assignment.title: Bariatric — selection, anatomy and complications
assignment.scopeIn: Bariatric procedure selection, altered anatomy, leaks, internal hernia, marginal ulcer, obstruction, dumping, post-bariatric hypoglycemia and procedure-specific deficiencies.
assignment.scopeOut: Generic PN/EN and micronutrient biology belong to nutrition-support-metabolism. Ordinary peptic ulcer belongs to stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.
assignment.priorityReason: Existing marginal-ulcer and hypoglycemia families leave operative anatomy and acute complications thin.
researchAgenda: Procedure anatomy and acute postoperative emergencies

recordedHolds.reason: Verify the repeat-dilation priority and the actual suitability boundaries for stent and operation in the recorded bariatric guidance; no session count or diameter rule is inferred.
The key prefers repeat graded gastrojejunal dilation over stenting/operation; direct priority and suitability verification is held.

decision.title: A changed course during marginal-ulcer treatment
fairness: The learner must distinguish healing of the ulcer surface from persistent/recurrent narrowing, then recognize that a trauma-limited first dilation is not established failure of a completed endoscopic course.

Repeat graded dilation is a defensible best next option among stenting and operative revision for the represented course. The transient response and single limited session supply the close alternative discriminator. No confident clinical error identified.
Retained liquids, stable physiology and absent adjacent leak are necessary safety/context observations rather than a named management instruction.

Importance: high for bariatric complications and treatment escalation. Realism: recurrent solid-food intolerance with a healed crater and residual stricture fits an outpatient bariatric-endoscopy reassessment.
suggestions: Retain the ulcer-healing observations, partial first-session treatment and transient response. Clinician sign-off should confirm the dilation-versus-stenting ranking and any necessary procedural safety detail.

holdDisposition.reason: The key prefers repeat graded gastrojejunal dilation over stenting/operation; direct priority and suitability verification is held.

frozenReferences.policy: Preserve every exact version and visible field; do not resolve the hold with generic first-line dilation support.

drift.disposition: Audit remains the exact 15 assigned variants. No added ownership inferred from unrelated topic integrations.

value.displayName: A changed course during marginal-ulcer treatment
value.presentation: {patientName}, a 49-year-old woman with a prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, was prescribed a PPI for a documented marginal ulcer and stopped NSAIDs. She now has progressively less tolerance of food and recurrent post-meal vomiting. Repeat outside endoscopy shows retained food above a narrowed gastrojejunal opening that the scope could not traverse. She is currently hemodynamically stable.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next plan fits {patientName}'s changed course?

answerChoices.label: Arrange bariatric endoscopic and surgical review
answerChoices.rationale: The obstructive findings place her outside routine initial medical management and require specialist reassessment of the complication.

answerChoices.label: Continue the unchanged PPI plan until routine follow-up
answerChoices.rationale: The original uncomplicated plan does not address progressive intolerance with a documented narrowed outlet.

answerChoices.label: Repeat an empiric H. pylori eradication course
answerChoices.rationale: No new infection evidence is supplied, and repeating infection treatment does not assess the new obstructive finding.

decisionNodes.explanation: Initial PPI treatment and contributor control apply to an uncomplicated marginal ulcer. Obstruction or a refractory/complicated course needs a pathway beyond routine initial medication management. This case does not prescribe a dilation technique or revisional operation.

terminalDispositions.clinicalRationale: The original uncomplicated plan does not address progressive intolerance with a documented narrowed outlet.

question.stem: Which thiamine plan best fits {patientName}'s neurological findings and intake during the hospitalization?

answerChoices.label: Start oral thiamine while the assay is pending
answerChoices.rationale: Prompt replacement is appropriate, but the record shows repeated vomiting after oral tablets and drinks. The route cannot be relied upon for this acute neurological presentation.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Prompt replacement is appropriate, but the record shows repeated vomiting after oral tablets and drinks. The route cannot be relied upon for this acute neurological presentation.

answerChoices.label: Start oral thiamine after assay confirmation
answerChoices.rationale: This both waits for biochemical confirmation despite the acute neurological concern and relies on a route repeatedly not retained. It reflects a diagnostic-certainty-and-oral-treatment plan that does not fit the recorded risk.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This both waits for biochemical confirmation despite the acute neurological concern and relies on a route repeatedly not retained. It reflects a diagnostic-certainty-and-oral-treatment plan that does not fit the recorded risk.

answerChoices.label: Start intravenous thiamine after assay confirmation
answerChoices.rationale: A pending biochemical result should not delay treatment when the risk history and neurological findings support acute thiamine deficiency.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A pending biochemical result should not delay treatment when the risk history and neurological findings support acute thiamine deficiency.

answerChoices.label: Start intravenous thiamine while the assay is pending
answerChoices.rationale: The acute neurological pattern after prolonged failed intake warrants prompt treatment, and repeated failed oral attempts favor the intravenous route without awaiting the assay.

question.explanation: Treat the suspected acute thiamine deficiency while the assay is pending. Repeated vomiting after drinks and tablets makes oral delivery unreliable, so intravenous replacement is the appropriate immediate route while the cause of vomiting is addressed. No replacement dose, glucose-delay rule or laboratory-turnaround cutoff is taught.

patient.presentation: {patientName}, a 49-year-old woman, attends clinic after an outside hospitalization for prolonged vomiting following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. You review the neurological changes that occurred before treatment of her gastrojejunal opening.

profiles.presentation: {patientName}, a 49-year-old woman, attends clinic after an outside hospitalization for prolonged vomiting following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. You review the neurological changes that occurred before treatment of her gastrojejunal opening.

proposals.currentUpdate: During that hospitalization, before endoscopic treatment of the gastrojejunal opening, she repeatedly vomited after attempted drinks and vitamin tablets. Inattention, a broad-based gait and abnormal eye movements developed. A thiamine sample had been sent; the laboratory result was pending. Intravenous fluids and investigation of the vomiting were underway.

keyFirstReviewChoices.distractorRationale: This both waits for biochemical confirmation despite the acute neurological concern and relies on a route repeatedly not retained. It reflects a diagnostic-certainty-and-oral-treatment plan that does not fit the recorded risk.

choiceRationales.correctUnder: Acute neurological deficiency is not suspected and oral intake is retained sufficiently for the clinically selected replacement plan.

choiceRationales.label: Start oral thiamine after assay confirmation

choiceRationales.temptation: Treat the suspected deficiency as a nonurgent laboratory diagnosis to be confirmed before an oral prescription.
choiceRationales.correctUnder: A different nonacute evaluation with retained oral intake permits a clinician to await appropriate testing before an oral replacement plan.

choiceRationales.label: Start intravenous thiamine after assay confirmation
choiceRationales.rationale: A pending biochemical result should not delay treatment when the risk history and neurological findings support acute thiamine deficiency.
choiceRationales.temptation: Require laboratory proof before committing to parenteral replacement because several deficiencies can cause neurological symptoms.
choiceRationales.correctUnder: A nonurgent diagnostic question lacks the clinical suspicion requiring immediate treatment; that is not this neurological course.

choiceRationales.label: Start intravenous thiamine while the assay is pending

choiceRationales.temptation: Requires deciding both when to treat and whether the recorded oral route can deliver treatment.
choiceRationales.correctUnder: Acute thiamine deficiency is suspected and oral intake cannot be relied upon.

reasoning.interpret: Recognize an acute neurological deficiency risk from failed intake and the observed cognitive, gait and eye findings; do not wait for the assay to establish that treatment is time-sensitive.
reasoning.apply: Use the failed oral attempts to choose prompt intravenous rather than oral treatment or delayed parenteral replacement.

reasoning.consequence: Choosing a route that is not retained or awaiting confirmation can delay effective replacement during a neurological complication.

answerChoices.label: Keep current protein intake; use lower-glycemic carbohydrate portions
answerChoices.rationale: Changing carbohydrate quality is appropriate, but 8 + 12 + 10 gives only 30 g of daily protein. That preserves a nutritional shortfall rather than meeting the minimum protein target in the PBH guidance.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Changing carbohydrate quality is appropriate, but 8 + 12 + 10 gives only 30 g of daily protein. That preserves a nutritional shortfall rather than meeting the minimum protein target in the PBH guidance.

answerChoices.label: Increase protein to 60 g/day; retain the liquid carbohydrate pattern
answerChoices.rationale: The protein target addresses adequacy, but retaining rapidly absorbed liquid carbohydrate does not address the observed episode pattern or the lower-glycemic strategy recommended for PBH.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The protein target addresses adequacy, but retaining rapidly absorbed liquid carbohydrate does not address the observed episode pattern or the lower-glycemic strategy recommended for PBH.

answerChoices.label: Increase protein to 60 g/day; use lower-glycemic carbohydrate portions

answerChoices.label: Keep current protein intake; retain the liquid carbohydrate pattern

question.explanation: The record totals 30 g of protein daily. PBH dietary guidance sets individualized protein targets of at least 60 g/day, with higher needs in some patients. The episode pattern also supports replacing rapidly absorbed liquid carbohydrate with controlled lower-glycemic portions. These are separate nutritional requirements; changing only one leaves the other problem.

Keeping the current protein intake while changing to lower-glycemic carbohydrate portions (current-solid) would then be the relevant plan rather than increasing protein to correct a shortfall.

answerChoices.rationale: The low overnight sensor values do not coincide with symptoms and disagree with simultaneous finger-stick results. They do not establish a fasting syndrome that should determine the first investigation of the separate postmeal spells.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The low overnight sensor values do not coincide with symptoms and disagree with simultaneous finger-stick results. They do not establish a fasting syndrome that should determine the first investigation of the separate postmeal spells.

question.stem: Which next plan best fits {patientName}'s symptoms, sleeve assessment and medication record?

answerChoices.label: Replace omeprazole with bedtime famotidine
answerChoices.rationale: Changing the drug class does not correct the represented administration problem with the PPI. The record does not yet establish failure of a properly timed PPI course.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Changing the drug class does not correct the represented administration problem with the PPI. The record does not yet establish failure of a properly timed PPI course.

answerChoices.label: Proceed to Roux-en-Y bypass conversion
answerChoices.rationale: Post-sleeve conversion can be considered for a suitable medically refractory course, but bedtime administration of this conventional PPI leaves a reversible treatment issue to address first.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Post-sleeve conversion can be considered for a suitable medically refractory course, but bedtime administration of this conventional PPI leaves a reversible treatment issue to address first.

answerChoices.label: Move omeprazole dosing before breakfast
answerChoices.rationale: The diary shows consistent use but timing remote from a meal. Optimizing the administration of conventional delayed-release omeprazole is the appropriate next step before declaring it refractory or changing category of care.

question.explanation: Daily use does not establish appropriate administration. For conventional delayed-release omeprazole, ACG recommends dosing 30-60 minutes before a meal rather than at bedtime. Correct the administration issue and assess response before declaring medical failure. The anatomical assessment is stated once and does not justify dilation of a patent sleeve.

proposals.objective: Interpret apparent post-sleeve treatment failure from actual drug administration and anatomy before choosing the next treatment plan.

question.stem: Which investigation best clarifies {patientName}'s continuing regurgitation before further post-sleeve treatment?

answerChoices.label: Ambulatory pH-only monitoring after PPI withdrawal
answerChoices.rationale: Off-therapy monitoring can establish an unproven diagnosis. Prior grade C esophagitis already provides objective GERD evidence, and this protocol does not answer the present on-treatment symptom question.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Off-therapy monitoring can establish an unproven diagnosis. Prior grade C esophagitis already provides objective GERD evidence, and this protocol does not answer the present on-treatment symptom question.

answerChoices.label: Ambulatory impedance-pH monitoring after PPI withdrawal
answerChoices.rationale: Adding impedance does not correct the mismatch in medication state. Off-therapy testing asks about untreated reflux rather than the relationship between symptoms and reflux during the recorded regimen.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Adding impedance does not correct the mismatch in medication state. Off-therapy testing asks about untreated reflux rather than the relationship between symptoms and reflux during the recorded regimen.

answerChoices.label: Ambulatory pH-only monitoring during PPI treatment
answerChoices.rationale: The medication state fits a persistent on-treatment question, but pH-only monitoring does not capture the full association with nonacid reflux that impedance-pH can evaluate.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The medication state fits a persistent on-treatment question, but pH-only monitoring does not capture the full association with nonacid reflux that impedance-pH can evaluate.

answerChoices.label: Ambulatory impedance-pH monitoring during PPI treatment
answerChoices.rationale: GERD is already objectively established, but the mechanism of the current symptoms during therapy remains unresolved. On-treatment impedance-pH evaluates their relationship with acid and nonacid reflux before another treatment decision.

question.explanation: The prior grade C esophagitis establishes GERD, but it does not prove that the current regurgitation during treatment has the same mechanism. ACG recommends on-therapy impedance-pH assessment for persistent symptoms in established GERD on twice-daily PPI. The on/off state and impedance/pH scope answer different questions. The result may inform later bariatric treatment; this item does not force an operation from an adequacy label.

proposals.objective: Use prior objective GERD evidence and current PPI exposure to select the reflux-monitoring protocol before further post-sleeve treatment.

answerChoices.label: Start oral thiamine while the assay is pending

answerChoices.rationale: Changing carbohydrate quality is appropriate, but 8 + 12 + 10 gives only 30 g of daily protein. That preserves a nutritional shortfall rather than meeting the minimum protein target in the PBH guidance.

answerChoices.label: Increase protein to 60 g/day; retain the liquid carbohydrate pattern
answerChoices.rationale: The protein target addresses adequacy, but retaining rapidly absorbed liquid carbohydrate does not address the observed episode pattern or the lower-glycemic strategy recommended for PBH.

answerChoices.label: Increase protein to 60 g/day; use lower-glycemic carbohydrate portions
answerChoices.rationale: This addresses both the measured protein shortfall and the association of episodes with rapidly absorbed liquid carbohydrate. The stated protein amount is the guideline minimum, with further individualization by the dietitian.

answerChoices.label: Keep current protein intake; retain the liquid carbohydrate pattern
answerChoices.rationale: This retains both the low protein total and the carbohydrate pattern associated with the recorded episodes. Each component requires correction rather than simple continuation.

decisionNodes.explanation: The record totals 30 g of protein daily. PBH dietary guidance sets individualized protein targets of at least 60 g/day, with higher needs in some patients. The episode pattern also supports replacing rapidly absorbed liquid carbohydrate with controlled lower-glycemic portions. These are separate nutritional requirements; changing only one leaves the other problem.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next investigation best evaluates {patientName}'s recurrent episodes after bypass?

answerChoices.label: Supervised fasting evaluation with venous biochemical sampling
answerChoices.rationale: The low overnight sensor values do not coincide with symptoms and disagree with simultaneous finger-stick results. They do not establish a fasting syndrome that should determine the first investigation of the separate postmeal spells.

answerChoices.label: Venous biochemical sampling during a typical spontaneous spell
answerChoices.rationale: The symptom diary and glucose log represent different events. Characterizing a typical symptomatic postmeal spell establishes the missing symptom-biochemistry relationship before assigning its cause.

answerChoices.label: Oral glucose tolerance testing with venous biochemical sampling
answerChoices.rationale: A standardized glucose load may provoke lows that do not establish what occurs during this patient's ordinary episodes. The current PBH guideline does not recommend OGTT diagnosis of PBH.

decisionNodes.explanation: Align symptoms and samples by episode. The asymptomatic overnight sensor values are not biochemical evidence for the daytime spells, and the normal clinic sample was obtained while she felt well. Obtain appropriate venous sampling during a typical spontaneous event. A low value by itself would still not complete the full etiologic evaluation or prove PBH.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next medication plan best fits {patientName}'s symptom and treatment course?

answerChoices.label: Continue the acarbose-based medication plan
answerChoices.rationale: The record shows benefit but also reproducible activity-limiting gastrointestinal effects that resolve on withdrawal and return on reintroduction. Persistence is not merely an untried first-drug stage.

answerChoices.label: Change to an oral diazoxide-based plan
answerChoices.rationale: Diazoxide is a later option. Intolerance of acarbose does not itself establish that the somatostatin-analogue stage is unsuitable or has failed.

answerChoices.label: Change to short-acting subcutaneous octreotide
answerChoices.rationale: The withdrawal/rechallenge course supports clinically important acarbose intolerance. Short-acting octreotide is a guideline-supported option when acarbose is ineffective or not tolerated.

decisionNodes.explanation: Fewer lows do not by themselves establish an acceptable medication response. The repeated gastrointestinal pattern on withdrawal and reintroduction supports acarbose intolerance. Consider a specialist-directed short-acting somatostatin analogue such as octreotide rather than insisting on the same drug or skipping directly to diazoxide. No dose, maximum trial count or universal adverse-effect cutoff is supplied.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: On admission, intermittent cramps had become continuous with repeated retching. His abdomen was tender without guarding; pulse was 96/min and blood pressure 122/76 mmHg. The record showed normal renal function and no prior contrast reaction.
decisionNodes.stem: Which initial study best fits {patientName}'s recorded acute presentation after gastric bypass?

answerChoices.label: Upper endoscopy of the pouch and anastomosis
answerChoices.rationale: Endoscopy assesses the pouch and gastrojejunal lumen, but it does not survey the entire altered mesenteric and intestinal anatomy needed for this acute pain course.

answerChoices.label: Computed tomography with oral and intravenous contrast
answerChoices.rationale: Contrast-enhanced CT surveys the altered bowel limbs, mesentery and possible extraluminal complications in this stable acute presentation.

answerChoices.label: Water-soluble contrast examination of the upper gastrointestinal tract
answerChoices.rationale: A luminal contrast study can assess proximal passage or leakage, but it provides less complete evaluation of the bowel and mesentery for the current acute course.

decisionNodes.explanation: The change to persistent acute pain after RYGB requires assessment beyond the pouch lumen. Contrast-enhanced CT with oral contrast evaluates the reconstructed bowel pathways and extraluminal anatomy. This is a review of the hospital investigation, not a clinic CT order.
sourceLabels: World Society of Emergency Surgery / IFSO; World Journal of Emergency Surgery (2022)

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: CT was acquired with oral and intravenous contrast and reviewed with the bypass operative report. It showed no fixed transition, no free air and no reported mesenteric swirl. Despite fluids and repeated reassessment, continuous pain and retching persisted and focal tenderness increased. Lactate remained within that laboratory's interval.
decisionNodes.stem: Which next hospital action best fits {patientName}'s continuing course after the CT?

answerChoices.label: Repeat contrast CT after another observation period
answerChoices.rationale: The first study was adequately acquired for the question. Another observation-and-scan cycle does not resolve the concerning persistent course and can delay recognition of an internal hernia.

answerChoices.label: Proceed to upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
answerChoices.rationale: Endoscopy is useful for a luminal source, but persistent acute symptoms after RYGB can arise from an internal hernia outside its field. The negative CT and normal lactate do not settle that risk.

answerChoices.label: Proceed to diagnostic surgical laparoscopy
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent acute pain and retching with increasing tenderness after RYGB justify prompt exploration despite inconclusive CT. A normal lactate is not evidence that the concerning course has resolved.

decisionNodes.explanation: A negative CT does not exclude an internal hernia after RYGB. The persistent acute symptoms and increasing tenderness justify prompt surgical exploration in the recorded hospital setting. Neither a normal lactate nor the absence of a reported swirl substitutes for clinical reassessment.

decisionNodes.stem: Which reconstructed intestinal pathway best explains {patientName}'s CT distribution after gastric bypass?

answerChoices.label: The alimentary limb at the jejunojejunostomy
answerChoices.rationale: This limb receives oral contrast from the pouch and is not the distended pathway in the report.

answerChoices.label: The common channel distal to the jejunojejunostomy
answerChoices.rationale: A downstream common-channel obstruction would not match selective upstream distension of the excluded pathway with an undistended alimentary limb.

answerChoices.label: The biliopancreatic limb at the jejunojejunostomy
answerChoices.rationale: The excluded stomach, duodenum and continuous proximal jejunum form the distended biliopancreatic pathway. The distribution localizes the obstruction toward its junction with the food stream.

decisionNodes.explanation: The patent food stream and selectively distended excluded stomach, duodenum and connected jejunum localize the problem to the biliopancreatic pathway toward the jejunojejunostomy. The distribution does not identify the exact obstructing lesion. This is a bounded anatomy-interpretation item retained as fair moderate application, not a claimed two-step treatment decision.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Endoscopy records distal esophageal mucosal breaks and a traversable sleeve without a fixed narrowing. She has been prescribed conventional delayed-release omeprazole. Her medication diary places the capsule at bedtime, several hours after her evening meal; she reports taking it every day. Heartburn and regurgitation continue.
decisionNodes.stem: Which next plan best fits {patientName}'s symptoms, sleeve assessment and medication record?

answerChoices.label: Replace omeprazole with bedtime famotidine
answerChoices.rationale: Changing the drug class does not correct the represented administration problem with the PPI. The record does not yet establish failure of a properly timed PPI course.

answerChoices.label: Proceed to Roux-en-Y bypass conversion
answerChoices.rationale: Post-sleeve conversion can be considered for a suitable medically refractory course, but bedtime administration of this conventional PPI leaves a reversible treatment issue to address first.

answerChoices.label: Move omeprazole dosing before breakfast
answerChoices.rationale: The diary shows consistent use but timing remote from a meal. Optimizing the administration of conventional delayed-release omeprazole is the appropriate next step before declaring it refractory or changing category of care.

decisionNodes.explanation: Daily use does not establish appropriate administration. For conventional delayed-release omeprazole, ACG recommends dosing 30-60 minutes before a meal rather than at bedtime. Correct the administration issue and assess response before declaring medical failure. The anatomical assessment is stated once and does not justify dilation of a patent sleeve.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: At a later visit, regurgitation continues. The earlier endoscopy documented Los Angeles grade C esophagitis. The dispensing and dosing records now show prescribed twice-daily delayed-release omeprazole, taken 30-60 minutes before breakfast and the evening meal, with refill and pill-count records matching use. A current endoscopy shows a traversable sleeve without a focal obstructing lesion. The team is evaluating whether the present symptoms remain reflux-related before further bariatric treatment.
decisionNodes.stem: Which investigation best clarifies {patientName}'s continuing regurgitation before further post-sleeve treatment?

answerChoices.label: Ambulatory pH-only monitoring after PPI withdrawal
answerChoices.rationale: Off-therapy monitoring can establish an unproven diagnosis. Prior grade C esophagitis already provides objective GERD evidence, and this protocol does not answer the present on-treatment symptom question.

answerChoices.label: Ambulatory impedance-pH monitoring after PPI withdrawal
answerChoices.rationale: Adding impedance does not correct the mismatch in medication state. Off-therapy testing asks about untreated reflux rather than the relationship between symptoms and reflux during the recorded regimen.

answerChoices.label: Ambulatory pH-only monitoring during PPI treatment
answerChoices.rationale: The medication state fits a persistent on-treatment question, but pH-only monitoring does not capture the full association with nonacid reflux that impedance-pH can evaluate.

answerChoices.label: Ambulatory impedance-pH monitoring during PPI treatment
answerChoices.rationale: GERD is already objectively established, but the mechanism of the current symptoms during therapy remains unresolved. On-treatment impedance-pH evaluates their relationship with acid and nonacid reflux before another treatment decision.

decisionNodes.explanation: The prior grade C esophagitis establishes GERD, but it does not prove that the current regurgitation during treatment has the same mechanism. ACG recommends on-therapy impedance-pH assessment for persistent symptoms in established GERD on twice-daily PPI. The on/off state and impedance/pH scope answer different questions. The result may inform later bariatric treatment; this item does not force an operation from an adequacy label.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Her Crohn's disease is being followed by the joint IBD and bariatric teams. Recent ileocolonoscopy shows no mucosal ulcers, CRP is within the laboratory interval and her weight and oral intake have been stable. Preoperative iron, folate, B12 and vitamin D measurements are within their laboratory intervals. She continues maintenance immunosuppression. She reports no reflux symptoms, and upper endoscopy shows no esophageal injury.
decisionNodes.stem: Which operation does conditional SAGES guidance favor for {patientName}'s bariatric discussion with Crohn's disease and prior ileal resections?

answerChoices.label: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass
answerChoices.rationale: RYGB may be considered in selected IBD patients, particularly with other competing indications. Prior small-bowel resection and continued immunosuppression strengthen concern about adding bypass here.

answerChoices.label: Sleeve gastrectomy
answerChoices.rationale: SAGES conditionally favors sleeve over RYGB in IBD. The prior bowel resections and immunosuppression strengthen that preference in this record, which has no competing reflux finding.

answerChoices.label: Duodenal switch reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: A markedly malabsorptive strategy adds further nutritional and bowel-reserve concerns. The same patient factors that strengthen the sleeve preference do not support choosing more bypass.

decisionNodes.explanation: For this bounded discussion, SAGES conditionally favors sleeve over bypass in IBD, with prior bowel resections and immunosuppression strengthening concern about additional bypass. The observed current disease/nutrition context is supplied, but this is not an instruction to operate regardless of the full assessment. Evidence is very low certainty, and different competing reflux or metabolic considerations can change the balance.

answerChoices.label: Serum copper assay; continue the extra supplement
answerChoices.rationale: Copper assessment fits the combined syndrome, but the labels show a substantial additional zinc exposure without a treatment indication. Continuing that exposure overlooks a possible contributor while evaluation proceeds.

answerChoices.label: Serum vitamin E assay; hold the extra supplement
answerChoices.rationale: Reviewing the extra zinc is sensible, and vitamin E can be relevant to neuropathy, but copper better integrates the cytopenias and this supplement exposure.

answerChoices.label: Serum vitamin E assay; continue the extra supplement
answerChoices.rationale: This does not best integrate either the cytopenias or the reconciled zinc exposure. The pattern warrants copper-focused evaluation and review of avoidable supplement excess rather than treating each finding in isolation.

answerChoices.label: Serum copper assay; hold the extra supplement
answerChoices.rationale: The neurological and hematological pattern supports copper assessment, while the labels show 15 + 2 x 50 = 115 mg/day of supplemental zinc. The self-started extra product is an avoidable exposure that can impair copper absorption; the prescribed multivitamin is a separate part of care.

decisionNodes.explanation: The cytopenias and sensory gait findings make copper assessment important. The label/use calculation gives 115 mg/day of supplemental zinc, including 100 mg from the self-started extra product. Excess zinc can impair copper absorption. Hold that nonindicated extra exposure while the clinical and laboratory evaluation proceeds; do not infer a proven copper diagnosis or a replacement dose from the pattern alone.

round2DraftEdits.currentUpdate: Endoscopy shows a clean-based ulcer on the jejunal side of a patent gastrojejunostomy. She has no melena or vomiting. She takes naproxen daily for knee pain and low-dose aspirin after a myocardial infarction. PPI treatment and bariatric follow-up are being started.
round2DraftEdits.task: Which medication plan best fits {patientName}'s current post-bypass ulcer findings?

choices.label: Withdraw naproxen and aspirin
choices.rationale: Removing naproxen addresses an avoidable ulcer exposure, but stopping secondary-prevention aspirin sacrifices a separate treatment benefit in this nonbleeding record. The shared PPI plan permits the indicated aspirin distinction to be considered.
choices.temptation: Apply an NSAID-avoidance rule to both medicines without weighing why each is taken.
choices.correctUnder: Aspirin lacks a continuing medical indication or the clinical antiplatelet assessment instead supports interruption.

choices.label: Continue naproxen and aspirin
choices.rationale: PPI treatment does not make chronic analgesic NSAID exposure an appropriate contributor to retain. The aspirin indication does not establish a comparable indication for naproxen.
choices.temptation: Assume acid suppression protects sufficiently to preserve both familiar medicines.
choices.correctUnder: A materially different specialist-assessed benefit-risk balance requires both medicines; no such naproxen requirement is represented here.

choices.label: Withdraw naproxen and continue aspirin
choices.rationale: Naproxen is the avoidable analgesic exposure. Aspirin has a secondary coronary-prevention purpose, which can justify continuation with the shared PPI plan in this nonbleeding setting.
choices.temptation: Requires separating avoidable ulcer risk from the competing benefit of another medicine in the same broad drug family.
choices.correctUnder: An uncomplicated nonbleeding marginal ulcer coexists with chronic analgesic NSAID use and medically indicated low-dose aspirin.

round2DraftEdits.explanation: Remove the avoidable naproxen exposure while retaining the secondary-prevention purpose of aspirin within the shared PPI plan. This is a nonbleeding marginal-ulcer medication decision, not a universal antiplatelet rule for hemorrhage.

reasoning.interpret: Identify the marginal ulcer and distinguish an avoidable analgesic exposure from secondary coronary prevention.
reasoning.apply: Reconcile the two medicines separately rather than withdrawing both or relying on PPI to preserve both.
reasoning.decidingObservation: Aspirin follows a myocardial infarction, whereas naproxen treats knee pain; the ulcer is clean-based without current bleeding.
reasoning.counterfactual: If aspirin had been self-started without a medical indication, withdrawing both would become reasonable. Active hemorrhage would require a separate antiplatelet assessment rather than carrying over this key.
reasoning.consequence: Blanket withdrawal can remove indicated cardiovascular prevention; continuing both retains an avoidable ulcer contributor.
reasoning.deletionTest: The redundant cardiology endorsement was deleted. The actual coronary indication, naproxen purpose and nonbleeding findings each distinguish the offered medication plans. Shared PPI care is stated once.
reasoning.cueAttack: The one v2 attempt removes the redundant aspirin endorsement and replaces the implausible foil as suggested. A subsequent cover-the-key component count still assembles the key from the majority withdrawal/continuation components in the three-plan set. An honest difficult or fair-moderate cue-resistant version was not established in this bounded attempt. Park rather than declare the remaining cue resolved; retain the supported medication fact and exact attempted wording for manager review.
reasoning.stageAudit: Three current medication-reconciliation plans with PPI and follow-up common to all.
reasoning.difficultyReason: The closest error is blanket NSAID-class withdrawal; the continue-both option tests overconfidence in PPI protection. No stretch difficulty is claimed.
reasoning.sequenceReview: The initial explanation does not name outlet dilation or later neurological replacement. The later outlet node receives its own chronology and findings.

choices.temptation: Treat continuing postmeal symptoms as evidence that the ulcer needs more of the original therapy.
choices.correctUnder: The outlet remains traversable and continuing symptoms track an active ulcer rather than a fixed obstructive opening.

choices.label: Perform surgical revision of the gastrojejunal anastomosis
choices.rationale: Revision is a real option after unsuccessful or unsuitable endoscopic treatment. The actual treatment record does not establish such an endoscopic failure.
choices.temptation: Treat inability of the scope to pass as sufficient evidence that reconstruction is required.
choices.correctUnder: Appropriate endoscopic treatment is unsuccessful or unsuitable, or an associated anatomical problem requires surgery.

choices.label: Perform through-the-scope endoscopic balloon dilation
choices.rationale: The surface response and persistent fixed lumen separate mucosal healing from mechanical recovery. Initial endoscopic dilation addresses this gastrojejunal stricture before unestablished refractory-stage revision.
choices.temptation: Requires interpreting the interval surface and transit findings before applying the actual treatment history.
choices.correctUnder: A suitable gastrojejunal stricture is at its first endoscopic treatment stage after the represented mucosal response.

round2DraftEdits.explanation: The prior ulcer surface has responded, but the fixed gastrojejunal opening still retains food. That distinction favors endoscopic balloon dilation rather than another ulcer-surveillance cycle. The record does not establish failed endoscopic treatment to justify moving directly to revision. This does not resolve the separately held recurrent-stricture v3 ranking.

reasoning.interpret: Distinguish improvement of the ulcer surface from persisting mechanical impairment of solid-food transit.
reasoning.apply: Use the actual treatment history to choose dilation rather than repeat ulcer-only care or unestablished refractory-stage revision.
reasoning.decidingObservation: The former crater is epithelialized while a fixed gastrojejunal opening retains food and blocks scope passage; the record lists medication rather than prior outlet treatment.
reasoning.counterfactual: If the gastrojejunal opening remained traversable and a persistent crater accounted for symptoms, continued PPI-based ulcer treatment and reassessment would become the better category of care. Documented unsuccessful endoscopic treatment could instead support revision.
reasoning.consequence: Equating a surface response with restored function can prolong obstruction; calling an untreated narrowing refractory can prompt avoidable escalation.
reasoning.deletionTest: The neutral task no longer announces outlet pathology or first-line stage. Both columns of the interval exhibit now determine the treatment category. The medication record determines stage. Liquid tolerance and hydration retain the clinic safety boundary.
reasoning.cueAttack: Named the gastrojejunal site in both examinations. Removed initial outlet intervention from the lead-in. A medical plan now competes with procedures, so interpreting the surface/lumen contrast changes the selected category; the key is not supplied by the task.
reasoning.stageAudit: Three next treatment plans for the same current symptoms; PPI remains shared background when procedural treatment is chosen.
reasoning.difficultyReason: The resident must distinguish mucosal response from a separate functional failure and then avoid premature operative escalation. The retained clinical observations make the question fair rather than obscure.
reasoning.sequenceReview: Prior ulcer feedback provides medication reconciliation but does not name a stricture or dilation. The current update and exhibit restate the anatomical site and chronology. The held N2 recurrence question remains untouched.

reviewResponse.clarity: Both exhibit columns and rows now name the gastrojejunal anastomosis/opening explicitly.
reviewResponse.cues: The lead-in no longer supplies a mechanical interpretation or initial-intervention category.
reviewResponse.fairness: The surface-versus-lumen evidence now selects the care category because continued ulcer therapy is an actual competitor. The treatment history and hydration observations remain visible.
reviewResponse.suggestions: Applied the neutral task, medical competitor and explicit anatomical naming in one v2 revision.

round2DraftEdits.currentUpdate: During that hospitalization, before endoscopic treatment of the gastrojejunal opening, she repeatedly vomited after attempted drinks and vitamin tablets. Inattention, a broad-based gait and abnormal eye movements developed. A thiamine sample had been sent; the laboratory result was pending. Intravenous fluids and investigation of the vomiting were underway.
round2DraftEdits.task: Which thiamine plan best fits {patientName}'s neurological findings and intake during the hospitalization?

choices.label: Start oral thiamine while the assay is pending
choices.rationale: Prompt replacement is appropriate, but the record shows repeated vomiting after oral tablets and drinks. The route cannot be relied upon for this acute neurological presentation.
choices.temptation: Choose prompt treatment but assume an oral prescription establishes effective delivery.
choices.correctUnder: Acute neurological deficiency is not suspected and oral intake is retained sufficiently for the clinically selected replacement plan.

choices.label: Start oral thiamine after assay confirmation
choices.rationale: This both waits for biochemical confirmation despite the acute neurological concern and relies on a route repeatedly not retained. It reflects a diagnostic-certainty-and-oral-treatment plan that does not fit the recorded risk.
choices.temptation: Treat the suspected deficiency as a nonurgent laboratory diagnosis to be confirmed before an oral prescription.
choices.correctUnder: A different nonacute evaluation with retained oral intake permits a clinician to await appropriate testing before an oral replacement plan.

choices.label: Start intravenous thiamine after assay confirmation
choices.rationale: A pending biochemical result should not delay treatment when the risk history and neurological findings support acute thiamine deficiency.
choices.temptation: Require laboratory proof before committing to parenteral replacement because several deficiencies can cause neurological symptoms.
choices.correctUnder: A nonurgent diagnostic question lacks the clinical suspicion requiring immediate treatment; that is not this neurological course.

choices.label: Start intravenous thiamine while the assay is pending
choices.rationale: The acute neurological pattern after prolonged failed intake warrants prompt treatment, and repeated failed oral attempts favor the intravenous route without awaiting the assay.
choices.temptation: Requires deciding both when to treat and whether the recorded oral route can deliver treatment.
choices.correctUnder: Acute thiamine deficiency is suspected and oral intake cannot be relied upon.

round2DraftEdits.explanation: Treat the suspected acute thiamine deficiency while the assay is pending. Repeated vomiting after drinks and tablets makes oral delivery unreliable, so intravenous replacement is the appropriate immediate route while the cause of vomiting is addressed. No replacement dose, glucose-delay rule or laboratory-turnaround cutoff is taught.

reasoning.interpret: Recognize an acute neurological deficiency risk from failed intake and the observed cognitive, gait and eye findings; do not wait for the assay to establish that treatment is time-sensitive.
reasoning.apply: Use the failed oral attempts to choose prompt intravenous rather than oral treatment or delayed parenteral replacement.
reasoning.decidingObservation: Drinks and tablets repeatedly return, and neurological changes develop while the assay remains pending.
reasoning.counterfactual: If oral intake were retained and the concern were a nonacute deficiency without neurological deterioration, a clinician-selected oral plan could be reasonable. Removing the clinical suspicion of acute deficiency would also change the urgency boundary.
reasoning.consequence: Choosing a route that is not retained or awaiting confirmation can delay effective replacement during a neurological complication.
reasoning.deletionTest: The backwards next-record transition was removed by making this a separate postdischarge review. Failed oral attempts determine route; the pending assay determines the timing comparison; the neurological observations establish urgency and are not hidden for difficulty.
reasoning.cueAttack: The task names thiamine because the scored decision is delivery and timing, not a vitamin-name association. The four route/timing plans balance oral/intravenous and pending/confirmed components twice each, so majority components cannot assemble the key. The neurological warning signs remain visible.
reasoning.stageAudit: Four replacement plans varying route and confirmation timing, with no invented doses or delays.
reasoning.difficultyReason: The nearest error gives the right nutrient promptly but through an unreliable route; the other error gives the right route after an inappropriate evidentiary delay. Recognition is intentionally not counted as a difficult standalone vitamin association.
reasoning.sequenceReview: This node is a self-contained clinic review of the hospitalization before gastrojejunal treatment. It no longer moves backwards inside the ulcer/endoscopy sequence.

reviewResponse.clarity: Moved the node into its own hospital-discharge review case; the presentation establishes the hospitalization, and the update places it before outlet treatment.
reviewResponse.cues: No clinical warning signs were deleted. The scored alternatives now make route and timing genuine choices rather than making every option parenteral.
reviewResponse.fairness: Retained inattention, gait and eye findings and failed intake. The pending sample does not become a reason to delay. No medication dose or arbitrary waiting period was introduced.
reviewResponse.suggestions: Used the suggested immediate replacement/timing comparison and explicitly supported oral-route failure; prediction reduced to fair moderate rather than claimed difficult association recall.
